# Methods

## Atrophy maps

We used openly shared, group-level deformation-based morphometry (DBM) maps comparing
patients with matched controls on the ICBM152 2009c nonlinear symmetric template (1 mm)
[29, 30, 32]: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from ADNI, and
frontotemporal dementia (FTD; pooled) and its clinical variants (behavioural-variant FTD,
bvFTD; semantic-variant primary progressive aphasia, svPPA; non-fluent variant, nfvPPA)
from NIFD/FTLDNI (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.7392621 and 10.5281/zenodo.10383493, CC-BY-4.0).
The source study reports 212 AD, 551 MCI and 125 FTD patients and 571 controls across
cohorts, modelled with mixed-effects models [29]; sample sizes for the variant maps were not
reported in the record. The variant maps span a much smaller numerical range (about ±1.5)
than the pooled FTD map (about ±16) and may therefore not be t-statistics; all analyses
below are invariant to linear rescaling. We define atrophy as −t, so that larger values mean
more volume loss. The three variant maps are likely to share one control group, which
inflates their mutual similarity; between-syndrome similarity is therefore reported only
descriptively. Parkinson's disease, available in the same record, was not analysed. No map
of dementia with Lewy bodies was available.

## Parcellation and template registration

Cortex was parcellated with the Schaefer 2018 atlas (7 networks; 400 parcels primary, 200
and 100 for robustness) [25]; subcortex with the Tian S1 atlas [26], whose 16 regions were
mapped onto the 14 structures of the ENIGMA connectomes (accumbens, amygdala, caudate,
hippocampus, pallidum, putamen and thalamus per hemisphere; anterior and posterior thalamus
merged) [27]. Both atlases are defined on FSL MNI152 (MNI152NLin6Asym), whereas the atrophy
maps are on ICBM152 2009c symmetric. We therefore registered the FSL MNI152 1 mm brain to the
ICBM 2009c symmetric brain (skull-stripped with the DBM brain mask) with ANTs symmetric
normalisation (SyN) [31] and warped both atlases with nearest-label interpolation onto the
grid of the maps. Registration raised the intensity correlation between the two templates
from 0.74 (world-coordinate resampling) to 0.91; 30% of cortical voxels changed parcel at
400 parcels (Supplementary Table S1).

Parcel values are mean −t within the parcel. Because DBM maps encode ventricular and sulcal
expansion that spreads into neighbouring tissue through smoothing, subcortical values were
taken from the core of each structure (voxels ≥ 3 mm from template CSF), which removed
spill-over that made the AD hippocampus appear only mildly atrophic (mean −t 1.6 with all
voxels, 3.0 in the core). The caudate remained dominated by ventricular expansion and is
flagged throughout. All parcels had ≥ 86% voxel coverage.

## Connectomes and distances

Group-level structural (SC) and functional (FC) connectivity from the Human Connectome
Project were taken from the ENIGMA toolbox for Schaefer-100/200/400 (cortex) and
Schaefer-400 with the 14 subcortical structures [27, 28]; label orders were verified to match
the atlases exactly. Negative SC weights (14 edges at 400 parcels; 20 with subcortex) were set
to zero. FC (negative values already set to zero upstream, density 97–99%) was used in full
and after proportional thresholding to its strongest 20% and 10% of edges.

Euclidean distances were computed between parcel centroids in ICBM 2009c space. Geodesic
distances along the cortical midthickness surface (fsaverage5, medial wall removed) were
computed between parcel centroid vertices with the heat method [33] (validated against the
analytic pole-to-pole distance on the sphere: 312 vs 314 mm); pairs in different hemispheres
have no cortical path.

## Predicting atrophy from other regions

For a weighting matrix M, the predicted atrophy of node i is the weighted mean of all other
nodes, P_i = Σ_{j≠i} M_ij a_j / Σ_{j≠i} M_ij, and the fit is r(a, P). With M = SC or FC this
is the neighbour atrophy of Zeighami et al. and Shafiei et al. [4, 5]. We compared:
(i) direct SC; (ii) five communication models on the SC [13]: shortest-path efficiency,
weighted communicability [15], search information (as the shortest-path probability 2^−SI)
[14], navigation efficiency with Euclidean greedy routing [12] and diffusion efficiency
(1/mean first-passage time); (iii) the network diffusion (heat) kernel e^{−βL} [3], β fitted;
(iv) FC (full, top 20%, top 10%); and two spatial baselines, (v) a Euclidean and (vi) a
geodesic distance kernel e^{−d/λ}, λ fitted. As a sensitivity analysis every communication
model received one fitted exponent (M^γ), matching the single parameter of the baselines.

Because a short-range kernel applied to a smooth map acts as spatial interpolation, we also
evaluated **distance-censored prediction**: all pairs closer than R mm (Euclidean; R = 10–60
mm) were removed from every model, so that a node's atrophy must be predicted from distant
nodes. Euclidean censoring is the conservative choice because volumetric smoothing acts in
Euclidean space and geodesic distances always exceed it within a hemisphere. The **unique
contribution** of a model beyond distance was measured as the partial correlation
r(a, P_M | P_distance), with λ refitted for every map and surrogate.

## Generative spreading from seeds

To evaluate spreading models in their generative form [3, 11], we seeded each model at every
node, alone and together with its contralateral homologue, and predicted the whole map:
network diffusion x(t) = e^{−Lt} x₀ on the SC (NDM-SC) or on the FC (NDM-FC), with L the
normalised graph Laplacian and t over 25 values (0.05–50), and isotropic spatial spread
e^{−d/λ} x₀ from the same seeds, in Euclidean or geodesic distance. For each model the best
seed and parameter were selected by maximising r(a, x).

## Null models and inference

Five null models were used. Three preserve the spatial autocorrelation of the map: spins of
the cortical surface with Hungarian reassignment [17–19] (subcortical nodes permuted among
themselves), variogram-matched surrogates [20] and Moran spectral randomisation [21]. Two
replace the SC while keeping the map: degree-preserving rewiring [22] and degree- and
geometry-preserving rewiring, in which swaps are accepted only within edge-length bins [23].
Every fitted parameter (λ, β, γ, t, best seed) was refitted inside each of the 1,000
surrogates or rewired networks per null. p-values are one-sided (null ≥ observed) for fits
and two-sided for paired differences between models; false discovery rate (FDR,
Benjamini–Hochberg) was controlled across syndromes × models within each null and radius.
A result was counted as evidence of a positive network constraint only if r > 0 and FDR
q < 0.05. Because geometry-preserving rewiring saturates at about 50% edge turnover, we also
report how it depends on the bin width (5–40 bins).

## Additional analyses

**Epicentres.** Nodes were ranked by the mean of their rank on atrophy and on SC-neighbour
atrophy [5], with spin and rewiring p-values. **Asymmetry.** Because Schaefer parcels are not
left–right homologous, each left parcel was compared with the identical region mirrored to
the right: the symmetric template allows the voxel map to be mirrored and re-parcellated with
the same atlas. **Hubs.** Node strength (SC; FC full and thresholded) was correlated with
atrophy (Spearman), with and without controlling for regional EPI signal (SPM12 mean EPI
template), a proxy for susceptibility dropout in orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex
[35]. **Eigenmodes.** Atrophy was reconstructed from the first K eigenmodes of the cortical
surface (Laplace–Beltrami, fsaverage5) [24] and of the SC and FC graph Laplacians, computed
within each hemisphere so that all bases have the same structure.

## Software and validation

Analyses used R 4.3 and Python 3.13. Network measures were implemented in an R package with
C++ kernels and validated against bctpy 0.6.1 and netneurotools 0.3.0 on the HCP
Schaefer-400 SC (maximum absolute difference ≤ 5×10⁻¹¹); spin permutations were validated
against neuromaps 0.0.7 (Supplementary Tables S2–S4). Code, intermediate data and validation
reports are available at the project repository.
